# Geometric closure of the remaining symmetric triangle sector

This file proves the geometric reduction to one explicit rational
inequality. That inequality is now proved, with a finite exact Bernstein
certificate, in exact-symmetric-triangle-chain-scalar-certificate-root.md.
The complete restricted theorem and dependency graph appear in
symmetric-common-vertex-triangle-chains-all-length-theorem.md.

The source, candidate, V, R, M and cap normalization are those of
symmetric-triangle-chain-shared-tilt-sectors-and-hinge-correction.md.
Normalize R=1. Thus M is the dimensionless sum of squared radii, and
actual cap masses are V times the displayed quantities. For the remaining
positive-normal sector define

    1/2<a<alpha=(9+sqrt(33))/24<2/3,
    c=1/(3a),             rho=1/[3(1-a)],
    A=a/(2a-1),
    L=(1-a)^2/[(2a-1)(2-3a)],
    B=(2a-1)/(2-3a),
    k_a(r)=A(r-c)_+^2-L(r-rho)_+^2,
    g=(2-3a)/[9(1-a)],
    lambda=(18a^3-24a^2+8a-1)/[27a^2(a-1)],
    v=(3a-1)(6a-1)/(27a^2),
    M0=9/2-1/[2a(1-a)],
    M1=g/(2/9-v),
    M2(b)=3/2+b+(5/2)b^2,       0<=b<=1.            (1)

All denominators are nonzero in the specified open a interval, and
2/9-v>0 there. The parameter lambda obeys lambda>2/9 and is not the
integer tilt. The actual tilt remains arbitrary throughout.

The proved scalar inequality, with every expression explicit, is

    g+(lambda-2/9)max{M0,M1,M2(b)}
      +k_a(b)-lambda[b^2+(1-b)^2/3]-2B E_a(b) >=0,   (S)

where

    E_a(b)=(1-b)^2/6,                              b>=rho;
    E_a(b)=(1-rho)^2/2-(1-rho)^3/[3(1-b)],          b<rho.       (2)

At b=1 the first branch is zero, so there is no 0/0 convention.
The two formulas agree at b=rho. The definition of k has the three
ordinary rational branches b<=c, c<=b<=rho, and b>=rho, agreeing at
both knots. At a approaching alpha, M1 diverges; no value at alpha
is requested in (S), since that endpoint is settled separately below.

The exact certificate in the cited scalar note proves(S) throughout
this real parameter domain, including every b boundary. Numerical
screens are not used in the proof.

## 1. The original shared-tilt cap has the required lower budget

The exact pair formula in the companion note says Q_a(r)=2k_a(r).
Its peak value and the exact own-fiber cap are

    k_a(1)=2/3-1/(9a),
    F_{a,1}(1/3)=1-1/[9a(1-a)]=k_a(1)+g.           (3)

Consequently EVERY original shared-tilt cap in this direction satisfies

    cap(a,tilt)/V >= g+sum_{j=-m}^m k_a(r_j).       (4)

No common realization of the separate pair optima is assumed. In fact
the companion note exhibits their monotonic mismatch. A lower bound
using these floors is valid for every tilt regardless of attainability.

## 2. A continuous polygonal comparison with its exact exponent

Direct integration of the two positive-part squares gives

    3 integral_0^1 k_a(r) dr=lambda.                (5)

Moreover k_a(r)/r^2 is nondecreasing on (0,1]. It is zero before c.
On c<r<rho it is A(1-c/r)^2, which increases. On rho<r<=1 it is

    (1/2)[1-(2/(3r)-a)^2/(a(2-3a))],

which increases since 2/(3r)-a>0. Continuity joins these assertions.
It follows that k_a(r)-lambda r^2 changes sign at most once, from
negative to positive. Its integral is zero by (5), so

    integral_b^1 [k_a(r)-lambda r^2] dr >=0
                 for every b in[0,1].             (6)

For a nonincreasing concave polygonal radius leg r(z), inverse-radius
density is a nonnegative nondecreasing finite step function of r,
with a possible initial plateau atom at r=1. As proved in Section3
of the companion note, integrating (6) against its upper-interval
step representation therefore yields

    integral_0^m k_a(r(z)) dz
         >=lambda integral_0^m r(z)^2 dz.          (7)

The plateau term is nonnegative because k_a(1)>=lambda: a nondecreasing
ratio is at least its r^2-weighted average at the upper endpoint.
Thus every plateau and every actual positive endpoint is included.

For completeness, the needed strict sign is exact:

    lambda-2/9
      =(2a-1)(6a^2-6a+1)/[27a^2(a-1)]>0,

since 6a^2-6a+1<0 on[1/2,2/3].

## 3. A sharp-enough finite trapezoid remainder

Let H(r)=(r-rho)_+^2. The function k_a+B H is convex on[0,1]:
its second derivative is zero before c, 2A on(c,rho), and zero
after rho; its first derivative is continuous at both knots. For
one linear interpolation cell with endpoints u>=w, the trapezoid
error consequently obeys

    error(k_a;u,w)>=-B error(H;u,w).                (8)

The errors are defined with the cell's real z-length one. For every
convex C1 piecewise C2 function H and u>w, its error is exactly

    error(H;u,w)
      =1/[2(u-w)] integral_w^u (s-w)(u-s)H''(s) ds. (9)

Formula (9) follows twice by integration by parts; H'' may be taken
piecewise, and H has no derivative jump here. A zero drop has zero error.
For each subinterval [u_{i+1},u_i] of[b,1], its kernel
(s-u_{i+1})(u_i-s)/(u_i-u_{i+1}) is no larger than the kernel
(s-b)(1-s)/(1-b). To check this, with fixed u the kernel
derivative with respect to w is -(u-s)^2/(u-w)^2<=0; with fixed w
its derivative with respect to u is (s-w)^2/(u-w)^2>=0. Thus moving
w downward or u upward increases the kernel.
Integrating over the disjoint subintervals in (9) proves

    sum_i error(H;r_i,r_{i+1}) <=error(H;1,b)=E_a(b). (10)

Direct evaluation gives exactly (2). When b>=rho, H is one quadratic
on the whole interval, giving (1-b)^2/6. When b<rho, H(b)=0,
H(1)=(1-rho)^2 and its average integral is
(1-rho)^3/[3(1-b)], giving the other branch.

Let T_k be the trapezoid sum over the polygonal leg. Summing (8) and
using (10) gives

    T_k >=integral_0^m k_a(r(z)) dz-B E_a(b).       (11)

The exact symmetric sums and the square quadrature identity are

    sum_{j=-m}^m k_a(r_j)=2T_k+k_a(b),
    M=2 integral_0^m r(z)^2 dz+b^2+(1/3)sum_i delta_i^2,
    sum_i delta_i^2 <=(1-b)^2,                      (12)

where delta_i=r_i-r_{i+1}>=0. Combining (7),(11),(12) proves the
unconditional, all-length scalar lower bound

    sum_j k_a(r_j)
      >=lambda[M-b^2-(1-b)^2/3]+k_a(b)-2B E_a(b).  (13)

Every integral in this argument is accompanied by its finite exact
quadrature error. It does not replace original mixed mass by continuous
volume, and it does not change the integer lattice or candidate point.

## 4. Two independent cap payments constrain any purported failure

First the own fiber alone has mass F_{a,1}(1/3) in this direction.
By (3), if cap/V <(2/9)M, then necessarily

    M>M0.                                         (14)

Second, because 0<=r<=1 and c<rho<1,

    (r-rho)_+ <=[(1-rho)/(1-c)](r-c)_+.

This is zero below rho, and above rho it is equivalent to r<=1.
The exact coefficient simplifies to

    k_a(r) >=K_a (r-c)_+^2,
    K_a=A-L[(1-rho)/(1-c)]^2
        =a(6a-1)/(3a-1)^2>0.                     (15)

The independently proved symmetric concave-sequence quadratic truncation
inequality gives sum(r_j-c)_+^2 >=(1-c)^3 M. Hence (4)-(15) give

    cap/V >=v M+g.                                (16)

For a<alpha, a purported failure therefore also forces M>M1.
For alpha<=a<2/3 one has v>=2/9, so (16) already proves the desired
inequality in that entire sector. At a=2/3, use the exact high-sector
formula and the same quadratic truncation theorem. Its factor is at
least1/4 for every a>=2/3, so these sectors are fully proved.

If m>=2, concavity gives r_1>=(1+b)/2 and r_2>=b. Thus

    M>=1+2r_1^2+2r_2^2>=M2(b).                     (17)

This last bound is unconditional and uses no failure assumption.
The inequalities (14) and M>M1 are conditional on a strictly bad cap.
Since lambda-2/9>0, (4),(13)-(17) imply that (S) would contradict any
such bad cap. Proving (S) is therefore sufficient to close the remaining
intermediate normal sector for every m>=2.

## 5. Boundary cases and the completed scalar dependency

The cases a=1/2 and a>=alpha are already proved as described above.
For m=0 the own centroid has depth4V/9, exceeding the half-mass target.
For m=1, the complete restricted theorem now gives a direct elementary
pair-floor calculation, with low-sector surplus13R^2/162, avoiding any
older three-fiber theorem. Its key inequality is
Q_a(r)>=(8R/3)(r-2R/3)_+, proved by one square on the middle branch
and a concave quadratic with nonnegative endpoints on the final branch.
Thus m=1 needs no use of M2(b), which would be false for that length.

The positive-normal reduction at the own centroid is already an exact
all-cap domination theorem for this source. The touching sampled radius
majorant is simply r_k<=R, with slope zero. It covers mixed-sign and
both-negative continuous normals by fiberwise simplex-vertex swaps
followed by one actual affine cap replacement. Vertical closed caps
can be dominated by a sufficiently tilted nonvertical cap, retaining
whole boundary fibers in the comparison. Coordinate symmetry then
puts the positive normal in the stated range. Therefore no original
normal sector beyond the one represented in (S) remains after the
geometric reductions.

The cited exact proof of(S), combined with the reductions above,
establishes the all-length symmetric common-vertex triangle-chain
theorem at the displayed actual own centroid. This does not establish
arbitrary nonsymmetric radius chains, arbitrary continuous dimension,
or OC in full.
